title: CompactionRL: Reinforcement Learning with Context Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents

paper.title: CompactionRL: Reinforcement Learning with Context Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Long-horizon agentic LLMs are increasingly limited by finite context windows, as extended interaction trajectories can exceed the maximum context length before a task is completed.
Context compaction offers a natural solution by summarizing previous interaction states and continuing the rollout under a compressed context, but incorporating compaction into reinforcement learning remains underexplored.
We propose CompactionRL, a reinforcement learning strategy to train long-horizon agentic LLMs with context compaction.
Our approach jointly optimizes task execution and summary generation with token-level loss normalization and cross-segment generalized advantage estimation.
This design enables the LLM agents to learn from compacted long-horizon trajectories.
We train CompactionRL on top of open models and observe consistent performance gains on agentic coding tasks.
CompactionRL enables the open GLM-4.5-Air model (106B-A12B) to achieve Pass@1 scores of 66.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 26.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, exceeding the base model under inference-time compaction by 6.6 and 4.9 points, respectively.
Built upon GLM-4.7-Flash (30B-A3B), CompactionRL improves Pass@1 by 5.5 and 6.7 points against the base model, reaching 56.0% on SWE-bench Verified and 20.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.0.
CompactionRL is thus deployed in the RL pipeline for training the open GLM-5.2 model (750B-A40B).

Context compaction offers a natural solution by summarizing previous interaction states and continuing the rollout under a compressed context, but incorporating compaction into reinforcement learning remains underexplored. We propose CompactionRL, a reinforcement learning strategy to train long-horizon agentic LLMs with context compaction. Our approach jointly optimizes task execution and summary generation with token-level loss normalization and cross-segment generalized advantage estimation. This design enables the LLM agents to learn from compacted long-horizon trajectories. We train CompactionRL on top of open models and observe consistent performance gains on agentic coding tasks. CompactionRL enables the open GLM-4.5-Air model (106B-A12B) to achieve Pass@1 scores of 66.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 26.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, exceeding the base model under inference-time compaction by 6.6 and 4.9 points, respectively. Built upon GLM-4.7-Flash (30B-A3B), CompactionRL improves Pass@1 by 5.5 and 6.7 points against the base model, reaching 56.0% on SWE-bench Verified and 20.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.0. CompactionRL is thus deployed in the RL pipeline for training the open GLM-5.2 model (750B-A40B). 1 1 footnotetext: Equal Contribution. 2 2 footnotetext: Work done while YL, ZH, and YJ interned at Z.AI. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to long-horizon interactive tasks, such as software engineering, terminal-based problem solving, and web interaction ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Nakano and others, 2021 ; Jimenez et al., 2023 ) . These tasks require agents to repeatedly reason, act, observe environment feedback, and revise their plans over many steps. As the interaction proceeds, the accumulated history, including tool outputs, intermediate reasoning, error messages, and partial solutions, can exceed the model’s finite context window. Although longer-context models alleviate this issue, scaling context length alone is costly and does not fully solve degraded utilization over long sequences ( Beltagy et al., 2020 ; Dao et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Hsieh et al., 2024 ) . Thus, long-horizon RL for LLM agents requires mechanisms that allow training to proceed under a fixed context budget. Context compaction provides a natural way to address this limitation. When the history approaches the context limit, earlier interaction history can be summarized into a shorter state, after which the agent resumes from the compacted summary and a small amount of recent context. Related ideas have been explored in language-agent memory, reflection, and long-horizon interaction systems ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2023 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . However, prior uses of compaction are mostly treated as inference-time heuristics or external memory operations. In RL training, compaction has a more fundamental role: once a summary replaces the original history, it determines what information is available for all subsequent actions. Therefore, task success depends not only on the execution policy, but also on the quality of the compaction policy. Context compaction introduces additional challenges for asynchronous agentic RL. First, differences in compaction frequency and subsequent execution length increase variation in rollout generation time. Group-relative methods such as GRPO must wait for the slowest rollout in each group to finish before computing advantages, increasing policy lag and off-policy effects ( Hou et al., 2026 ) . Second, jointly optimizing task execution and summarization requires including both execution and summary segments in training despite summary segments being substantially shorter, creating a severe length imbalance that can lead to disproportionate weighting under segment-level loss. Third, computing GAE independently within each segment places the shared terminal reward at local segment boundaries, artificially shortening its temporal distance from earlier actions and summaries and distorting temporal credit assignment. In this work, we propose CompactionRL, a PPO-based reinforcement learning framework for building long-horizon agentic LLMs with trainable context compaction, as shown in Figure 1 . CompactionRL incorporates compaction into rollout sampling, reconstructing the agent context from a summary once context budget is exhausted. Its core strategy is to jointly optimize task execution actions and summarization actions under the same final task reward. This enables RL training horizon to extend beyond the peak context length while keeping the actual working context budget fixed. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Figure 1: Left: Context compaction allows execution to continue under a fixed context window by initiating a new trace from a compressed summary once the context budget is exhausted. Without compaction, execution terminates upon exhaustion of the context budget. Right: Performance on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 across the base model with inference compaction, standard no-compaction RL, RL with inference compaction, and CompactionRL. “Base Model + Infer. Comp.” denotes the base model evaluated with context compaction. “RL” denotes standard RL trained and evaluated without compaction, while “RL + Infer. Comp.” uses the same RL checkpoint but enables context compaction during evaluation. • We bring context compaction into long-horizon agentic RL training. We adopt single-rollout PPO to avoid waiting for rollout groups, which is a problem more severe in compaction-aware training, and reduce the associated policy lag in asynchronous training, while using a learned critic to estimate token-level advantages for execution and summarization segments. • We develop CompactionRL to jointly train trajectory generation and summary generation with a shared task-level reward, making summarization a learned part of the model rather than an inference-time heuristic. To handle compacted rollouts, we use token-level loss normalization to reduce length-induced weighting bias and cross-segment GAE to preserve temporal credit assignment across compaction boundaries. • CompactionRL achieves consistent gains on long-horizon agentic coding tasks. Compared with the base model with inference-time compaction, CompactionRL improves GLM-4.7-Flash by 5.5 5.5 points on SWE-bench Verified and 6.7 6.7 points on Terminal-Bench 2.0. It also improves GLM-4.5-Air by 6.6 6.6 and 4.9 4.9 points on the two coding benchmarks, respectively. These results show that RL-trained compaction can extend the effective training horizon of agentic LLMs without increasing the maximum working context length. 2 Related Work Context Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents. Long-horizon language agents must maintain task-relevant state across extended sequences of reasoning, tool calls, and environment feedback. A standard ReAct-style agent appends the full interaction history to the prompt ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , but this makes the context grow with the trajectory and can reduce both efficiency and effective information use in long contexts ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Prior work has addressed this issue through longer-context modeling and evaluation ( Bai et al., 2024 ; Hsieh et al., 2024 ) , prompt or observation compression ( Jiang et al., 2023b ; Jiang et al., 2023a ) , and explicit memory or reflection mechanisms ( Packer et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) , showing that compressing or externalizing history can extend the effective horizon of LLM agents. Recent work has begun to incorporate context management into agent training. SUPO ( Lu et al., 2025 ) and Memex(RL) ( Wang et al., 2026 ) introduce context management into multi-turn RL and optimize with GRPO, without considering context state differences across compaction segments for advantage calculation; ReSum ( Wu et al., 2025 ) trains on segmented trajectories without optimizing the summarizer while Yi et al. (2026) and Wu et al. (2026) train only the context manager. However, how to jointly train long-horizon coding agents with both execution and compaction segments remains underexplored. Reinforcement Learning for Language Models. Reinforcement learning has become a central technique for improving language models with outcome feedback ( Uesato et al., 2022 ) . Early RLHF systems commonly adopt PPO with an explicit value function ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang and others, 2022 ) , while recent reasoning-oriented LLM training often favors critic-free or group-relative objectives such as RLOO, GRPO, and DAPO ( Ahmadian and others, 2024 ; Shao and others, 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Hou et al., 2025b ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) that have shown strong performance on verifiable-reward tasks such as mathematical reasoning and coding ( Hou et al., 2025a ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . At the same time, recent studies show that critic-based methods can still be highly effective when value learning is carefully designed. VC-PPO ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) improves PPO through value pretraining and modified advantage estimation and VAPO ( Yue et al., 2025 ) demonstrates that a value-based RL framework can achieve strong and stable reasoning performance. SAO ( Hou et al., 2026 ) adopts single-rollout sampling to reduce policy lag caused by waiting for complete rollout groups in asynchronous agentic RL. These studies motivate critic-based optimization for long-horizon agents, supporting both state-dependent advantage estimation and training without group-relative baselines. 3 The CompactionRL Method We present CompactionRL, a reinforcement learning framework for long-horizon language agents under a fixed context budget. The central idea is to make context compaction part of rollout sampling: when the interaction history approaches the context limit, the agent produces a compact summary of the previous trajectory and then resumes from a reconstructed context containing the summary and a short history tail of recent interaction. The summary is generated by the trainable policy and is optimized together with ordinary task-execution actions under the final task reward. Figure 2 gives an overview of the framework. Figure 2: Overview of CompactionRL. During rollout collection, the agent interacts with the environment under a fixed context budget. When the remaining context budget falls below a compaction threshold T comp T_{\mathrm{comp}} , the policy generates a summary and resumes from the summary and recent turns. All execution and summary segments are optimized and share the trajectory reward R R . During training, we propagate this reward across segment boundaries by correcting the local GAE advantage A s , i loc A^{\mathrm{loc}}_{s,i} with the number of optimized tokens in subsequent segments, N > s N_{>s} , yielding the cross-segment advantage A ^ s , i \widehat{A}_{s,i} . Standard RL without compaction optimizes each rollout as a single execution segment. 3.1 Trainable Context Compaction Compaction during Rollout Sampling. We represent the interaction history as h t = ( s , u , z 1 , … , z t ) , z i = ( a i , o i ) , h_{t}=(s,u,z_{1},\ldots,z_{t}),\qquad z_{i}=(a_{i},o_{i}), (1) where s s is the system prompt, u u is the original user instruction, a i a_{i} is the assistant response at step i i , and o i o_{i} is the corresponding environment observation. We treat each assistant-observation pair z i z_{i} as an atomic step, so that tool calls and their feedback are not separated by compaction. Let C C denote the context budget and | h t | |h_{t}| the token length of the current history, Compaction is triggered when the remaining context budget falls below a threshold T comp T_{\mathrm{comp}} : C − | h t | < T comp . C-|h_{t}|<T_{\mathrm{comp}}. (2) Once triggered, we append a fixed summarization instruction q sum q_{\mathrm{sum}} to the current history and sample a summary S t S_{t} from the policy, where q sum q_{\mathrm{sum}} asks the model to preserve information necessary for continuing the task, including the original goal, completed actions, important observations, unresolved errors, current state, and plausible next steps. After summary generation, the rollout continues from a reconstructed context h ¯ t = s ⊕ u resume ​ ( S t ) ⊕ ( z t − k + 1 , … , z t ) , \bar{h}_{t}=s\oplus u_{\mathrm{resume}}(S_{t})\oplus(z_{t-k+1},\ldots,z_{t}), (3) where u resume ​ ( S t ) u_{\mathrm{resume}}(S_{t}) is a fixed template containing the generated summary. The final term keeps the most recent k k turns while the summary covers only the history preceding the k k turns. We use k = 2 k=2 by default and reduce k k when necessary to ensure that h ¯ t \bar{h}_{t} fits within the context budget. This reconstruction preserves long-range information through S t S_{t} while retaining the most recent environment state exactly. Training Segments. Compaction naturally partitions a rollout into a sequence of trainable segments, τ = ( σ 1 , … , σ K ) , \tau=(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{K}), (4) where each segment is either an execution segment or a summarization segment. An execution segment contains tokens produced for solving the task, while a summarization segment contains the summary tokens generated before context reconstruction. Summary tokens are sampled from the same trainable policy and are included in the RL objective. Each rollout receives a final task reward R ⁡ ( τ ) R(\tau) determined by task correctness. We assign this rollout-level reward to all trainable segments from the same rollout. We do not introduce a separate summary-quality reward, since hand-designed summary metrics may not reflect which details are useful for continuation. Effect of Summarization Quality. Compaction makes task success sensitive to the quality of the summary. A summary that omits a crucial file path, error message, failed command, or partial solution can make subsequent actions ineffective even when the execution policy itself is strong. To quantify this effect, we fix the execution agent and vary only the summary agent. Table 1: Effect of summarization quality under context compaction. The execution agent is fixed to GLM-4.7-Flash, while tested with various summary agents including Qwen3.5-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) and Qwen3-30B-A3B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . SWE-Verified Acc. denotes pass@1(%) on SWE-bench Verified; Summary Count / Trace reports the average number of summaries triggered per trace. Execution Agent Summary Agent SWE-Verified Acc. Summary Count / Trace GLM-4.7-Flash Qwen3.5-27B 55.5 1.010 GLM-4.7-Flash GLM-4.7-Flash 50.5 1.075 GLM-4.7-Flash Qwen3-30B-A3B 49.0 1.126 Table 1 shows that changing only the summary agent leads to a large difference in final task performance. The best summarizer improves SWE-Verified accuracy from 49.0 49.0 to 55.5 55.5 , a gain of 6.5 6.5 absolute points, while also triggering slightly fewer compactions per trace. This result suggests that compaction is a performance-critical decision process rather than a passive preprocessing step. We therefore train summary generation jointly with task execution. 3.2 Optimization under Compacted Rollouts Single-Rollout Optimization. Compaction increases variation in rollout generation time since rollouts differ in compaction frequency and subsequent execution length. Group-relative advantage estimation requires completed rollouts to wait for the slowest member of the group, while asynchronous policy updates increase the mismatch between rollout and training policies during this waiting period. Following SAO ( Hou et al., 2026 ) , we adopt PPO with one rollout per prompt to avoid this additional waiting and reduce the associated off-policy effects. Moreover, resumed segments condition on different compacted histories. A learned critic provides context-dependent value estimates for token-level advantage estimation, whereas rollout-level group normalization does not explicitly account for these intermediate states differences. Token-Level Loss for Length Imbalance. Since the length of agent trajectories and summarization varies significantly, we choose to use token-level loss instead of sequence-level loss to overcome the severe imbalance. Let ℳ \mathcal{M} denote the set of optimized assistant-token positions in a training batch. For token y s , i y_{s,i} in segment σ s \sigma_{s} , conditioned on context x s , i x_{s,i} , let ρ s , i ​ ( θ ) \rho_{s,i}(\theta) denote the importance sampling ratio of the current policy π θ \pi_{\theta} to the rollout policy π θ old \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} . We optimize the clipped PPO objective ℒ π = − 1 | ℳ | ∑ ( s , i ) ∈ ℳ min ( ρ s , i ( θ ) A ^ s , i , clip ( ρ s , i ( θ ) , 1 − ϵ , 1 + ϵ ) A ^ s , i ) , \mathcal{L}_{\pi}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}\sum_{(s,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\min\left(\rho_{s,i}(\theta)\widehat{A}_{s,i},\mathrm{clip}\left(\rho_{s,i}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)\widehat{A}_{s,i}\right), (5) where ϵ \epsilon is the clipping threshold and A ^ s , i \widehat{A}_{s,i} is the advantage estimate described below. The loss computation is performed over generated tokens rather than over samples. This is important because compaction introduces heterogeneity in both segment count and segment length. Segment-level averaging would make a rollout with more compaction events contribute more strongly than a rollout with fewer segments, even when both receive the same task reward. Token-level normalization removes this segment-count bias and gives each trainable token equal weight. Cross-Segment Generalized Advantage Estimation. PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) uses a learned critic V ϕ V_{\phi} to estimate expected discounted returns. The temporal-difference (TD) residual measures the discrepancy between the one-step bootstrapped return and the current value estimate: δ t = r t + γ ​ V ϕ ​ ( x t + 1 ) − V ϕ ​ ( x t ) , \delta_{t}=r_{t}+\gamma V_{\phi}(x_{t+1})-V_{\phi}(x_{t}), (6) where x t x_{t} is the current context, r t r_{t} is the reward, and γ \gamma is the discount factor. Generalized advantage estimation (GAE) ( Schulman et al., 2015 ) computes token-level advantages by accumulating subsequent TD residuals: A t GAE = ∑ ℓ = 0 T − t ( γ ​ λ ) ℓ ​ δ t + ℓ , A_{t}^{\mathrm{GAE}}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{T-t}(\gamma\lambda)^{\ell}\delta_{t+\ell}, (7) where T T is the number of optimized tokens and λ \lambda is the trace parameter. This accumulation propagates delayed task feedback to earlier tokens while discounting more distant residuals. Compacted rollouts also create a temporal credit-assignment issue. Since each segment is optimized independently, a naive segment-level GAE computation places the shared terminal reward at the end of every segment. For earlier segments, this makes the final task outcome appear artificially closer than it is in the original rollout, over-crediting actions or summaries that occur far before task completion. For a segment σ s \sigma_{s} with n s n_{s} optimized tokens, the local GAE estimator is A s , i loc = ∑ ℓ = 0 n s − i ( γ ​ λ ) ℓ ​ δ s , i + ℓ , δ s , i = r s , i + γ ​ V ϕ ​ ( x s , i + 1 ) − V ϕ ​ ( x s , i ) , A^{\mathrm{loc}}_{s,i}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{n_{s}-i}(\gamma\lambda)^{\ell}\delta_{s,i+\ell},\qquad\delta_{s,i}=r_{s,i}+\gamma V_{\phi}(x_{s,i+1})-V_{\phi}(x_{s,i}), (8) where i i indexes tokens within the segment. Let N > s = ∑ j > s n j N_{>s}=\sum_{j>s}n_{j} be the number of optimized tokens generated after segment σ s \sigma_{s} in the same rollout. We apply a trajectory-position correction A ^ s , i = ( γ ​ λ ) N > s ​ A s , i loc . \widehat{A}_{s,i}=(\gamma\lambda)^{N_{>s}}A^{\mathrm{loc}}_{s,i}. (9) This correction discounts earlier segments according to the number of subsequent trainable tokens before rollout termination. In particular, if the terminal task reward appears at the last token of each independently optimized segment, then the reward term for token ( s , i ) (s,i) receives discount ( γ ​ λ ) N > s + n s − i , (\gamma\lambda)^{N_{>s}+n_{s}-i}, (10) which matches its distance to the final outcome in the concatenated compacted rollout. Note that this is an approximation rather than an exact reconstruction of full-trajectory GAE. Since an exact reconstruction of full-trajectory GAE would require recursively propagating TD residuals from later to earlier compaction segments, introducing cross-segment dependencies that preclude parallel processing within a batch, we use the trajectory-position correction above instead of exact reconstruction to preserve training efficiency. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Training Details. We conduct experiments with two models at different parameter scales: GLM-4.7-Flash and GLM-4.5-Air-SFT. The latter is obtained by supervised fine-tuning GLM-4.5-Air ( GLM et al., 2025 ) on trajectories generated by GLM-4.7. For each model, we initialize the corresponding critic from the same model checkpoint and perform 50 steps of value pretraining on the training dataset before reinforcement learning. We use open-source training data from SWE-Dev ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . For the training of CompactionRL, we use slime ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , an open-source asynchronous RL framework, for reinforcement learning training. For RL training, we employ a global batch size of 128, sample one rollout per prompt, and use context budgets of 64k for GLM-4.7-Flash and 80k for GLM-4.5-Air-SFT. The policy is optimized with Adam using a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} , while the critic is trained with a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} . For advantage estimation, we set the reward discount factor γ = 1 \gamma=1 and adopt length-adaptive GAE ( Yue et al., 2025 ) with λ = 1 − 1 α ​ l \lambda=1-\frac{1}{\alpha l} and α = 1.5 \alpha=1.5 , where l l denotes the response length. To ensure that the critic keeps pace with policy updates, we perform two value model updates and one policy update for each batch, facilitating accurate advantage estimation. Each assistant response is limited to 10,240 tokens and compaction is triggered when the remaining context budget falls below 10,240 tokens, with at most three compaction operations per rollout. Detailed model configurations and compute resources are provided in Appendix A.2 . Evaluation Setting. We evaluate CompactionRL on SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2023 ) and Terminal-Bench 2.0 ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) , using 200 randomly sampled tasks from SWE-bench Verified and the full Terminal-Bench 2.0 set, and report Pass@1 accuracy. The complete list of sampled tasks is provided in Appendix A.1 . All evaluations are conducted in the Harbor ( Harbor Framework Team, 2026 ) environment with the Terminus-KIRA ( KRAFTON AI and Ludo Robotics, 2026 ) agent scaffold. Evaluation hyperparameters include: top- p = 1.0 p=1.0 , temperature = 1.0 =1.0 , up to 250 interaction turns and at most three compaction operations per trajectory. 4.2 Main Results Table 2 compares the base models, standard no-compaction PPO , CompactionRL (w/o sum. loss), and the full CompactionRL under single-window or compacted evaluation settings on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0. CompactionRL (w/o sum. loss) enables compaction during RL but masks the loss on summary-response turns, separating the effect of training on compacted histories from that of directly optimizing the summarizer. CompactionRL achieves the best performance across both model scales and benchmarks. Inference-time compaction generally improves the base models by extending their effective context budget. Standard PPO improves single-window execution, but this benefit does not transfer consistently to compacted inference, where it either degrades performance or yields smaller gains than CompactionRL. Moreover, the consistent improvements of CompactionRL over CompactionRL (w/o sum. loss) across both model scales and benchmarks demonstrate the benefit of directly optimizing summarization during compaction-aware training. Overall, these results indicate that CompactionRL effectively extends the usable context horizon through trainable compaction. Table 2: Main results on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0. In all our results, SWE-bench Verified is evaluated on a random 200-instance subset, while public baselines are reported on the full benchmark. The public baselines are taken from model cards or public reports and are included for reference only, as their agent scaffolds may differ from ours. 4.3 Ablation Studies Effect of PPO. To evaluate the role of PPO in compaction-aware training, we compare CompactionRL with a GRPO-based baseline implemented following SUPO ( Lu et al., 2025 ) . Both methods jointly optimize task execution and summary generation, but SUPO computes group-relative advantages at the rollout level and assigns them uniformly to all compaction segments, whereas CompactionRL uses a learned critic to estimate token-level advantages. As shown in Table 3 , CompactionRL outperforms the SUPO baseline by 4.6 and 4.9 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0, respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness of critic-based PPO training. Effect of Token-Level Loss and Cross-Segment GAE. We further ablate the two optimization components designed for compacted trajectories using GLM-4.5-Air-SFT: token-level loss normalization and cross-segment GAE. As shown in Table 3 , removing either component degrades performance, confirming that both loss weighting and cross-segment credit assignment are important for compaction-aware RL. A larger degradation is observed when token-level loss normalization is removed, suggesting that correcting the optimization bias induced by variable segment counts and lengths is particularly critical. We further compare CompactionRL with standard no-compaction RL using an extended context window of 160k, which simulates access to a sufficiently long context that can retain the full trajectory without compaction-induced information loss. Figure 3 (a,b) shows that CompactionRL requires fewer compactions and tool calls than GLM-4.5-Air and CompactionRL (w/o sum. loss) but more than standard no-compaction RL. This indicates that CompactionRL learns both to exploit the extended context horizon enabled by compaction and a higher interaction efficiency, suggesting that the improvement is not attributable to longer interaction traces alone; rather, trained summaries help retain task-relevant information and reduce redundant re-exploration after compaction. (a) Summary length (b) Reasoning tokens per turn (c) Entropy Figure 4: Training dynamics of GLM-4.5-Air CompactionRL. (a) Summary optimization leads to increasingly longer and more detailed summaries. (b) CompactionRL increases reasoning tokens per turn. (c) Policy entropy. Figure 4 (a) analyzes the change of summary length during GLM-4.5-Air CompactionRL training. Compared with CompactionRL (w/o sum. loss), whose summary length decreases during training, CompactionRL produces increasingly longer and more detailed summaries when summary responses are included in the RL objective. This results in more complete and actionable compacted states that better preserve implementation-relevant context and continuation state. This suggests that optimizing summary responses encourages the model to retain useful detailed information for post-compaction continuation, rather than merely recording high-level task progress. We further quantify summary faithfulness and continuation usefulness in Appendix C , supporting that CompactionRL learns to generate summaries of higher quality. Figure 4 (b) further shows that the reasoning tokens of CompactionRL increase throughout training, whereas those of CompactionRL (w/o sum. loss) and standard no-compaction RL decrease. This indicates that learned compaction effectively expands the usable context window, allowing for more reasoning budget. Figure 4 (c) shows that CompactionRL also exhibits a slower entropy increase, suggesting more controlled policy optimization. Additional analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity is provided in Appendix B . 5 Conclusion We presented CompactionRL, a PPO-based framework that trains long-horizon agents with context compaction by optimizing execution and summary tokens under the same task reward. With token-level loss normalization and cross-segment GAE, CompactionRL improves SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 performance under a fixed peak context budget, while further ablations show that summary training produces more detailed compacted states and is important for these gains. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating context compaction into RL training for long-horizon agents, rather than treating it solely as an inference-time heuristic. Limitations. CompactionRL is designed for settings where context compaction is available during both training and inference. Extending its benefits to single-window inference requires further study, as the gains observed under compaction-enabled evaluation do not consistently transfer to this setting. In addition, cross-segment GAE remains an approximation to full-trajectory credit assignment, motivating further investigation into more precise reconstruction. We identify three recurring failure modes in lower-quality summaries: (1) omitted or misdiagnosed failures, where the summary records that tests failed but preserves an incorrect diagnosis; (2) stale or misrepresented repository states, where temporary debugging choices are mistaken for the final solution; and (3) premature completion claims, where passing tests are treated as sufficient even though the implementation still violates an explicit task requirement. In a representative comparison, RL (w/o compaction training) treats an earlier database failure as the current test status despite a later successful test run, causing the post-compaction agent to continue debugging an obsolete issue and ultimately fail. By contrast, CompactionRL preserves a more detailed account of the execution state, including which file-writing attempts failed, how these failures corrupted the source file, and why the task remained incomplete. These details guide the post-compaction agent to recover the file, complete the required modification, and verify the solution.
